blocks.text: A wound dressing set is a collection of sterile instruments and consumables used to clean, inspect, protect and dress wounds while minimising contamination and promoting healing.
It is commonly used for postoperative wounds, traumatic wounds, ulcers, burns and selected infected wounds.
The set may contain dressing forceps, gauze, a sterile drape, a receiver or kidney dish, a gallipot and other supplies. The exact contents vary according to the type of dressing required.
OSCE identification statement:

“This is a wound dressing set, used for the aseptic cleaning, inspection and dressing of wounds. It contains instruments and materials for removing old dressings, handling sterile dressings, applying prescribed wound-care solutions and protecting the wound.”
The following are common components, although not every set contains all of them.

rows: Hold and manipulate gauze, swabs and dressings.

Absorb fluid, clean the surrounding skin and assist with wound care.
Holds a small quantity of prescribed solution.

blocks.text: Additional items may include saline, a wound irrigation device, an appropriate waste bag and a dressing removal tool.
Usually have smooth or blunt gripping tips and are suitable for handling gauze and dressings without unnecessarily damaging tissue.
Have interlocking teeth designed for a firmer grip on tissue. They are not the routine first choice for handling delicate granulation tissue.

OSCE tip: A wound dressing pack is not necessarily a complete surgical instrument tray. It may contain disposable plastic forceps rather than metal instruments, and some supplies may need to be added separately.
A suitable wound dressing set should have the following characteristics:
Sterility: Instruments and materials contacting the wound should be sterile when required by the procedure.
Biocompatibility: Dressings and materials should be suitable for contact with the wound.
Absorbency: Gauze and absorbent pads should manage wound exudate appropriately.
Atraumatic handling: Instruments should allow gentle handling of dressings and tissue.
Appropriate packaging: Sterile packs should remain intact until use.
Ease of use: Components should be arranged for efficient aseptic handling.
Compatibility: Cleaning solutions and dressings should be appropriate for the wound and prescribed treatment.
Waste management: The set-up should permit safe disposal of contaminated materials.
The dressing set contains instruments, but the dressing material selected depends on the wound.
Examples: Gauze and absorbent pads.
Uses: Protecting wounds and absorbing exudate.
Limitation: Some gauze can adhere to the wound bed and cause trauma during removal.
Designed to reduce adherence to the wound surface.
Uses: Selected superficial wounds, fragile skin and wounds where atraumatic removal is important.
Examples: Foam, hydrocolloid, hydrogel and alginate dressings.
Uses: Selected wounds with different moisture-management requirements.
Limitation: Each dressing has specific indications and may be unsuitable for particular wound conditions.
Thin, transparent dressings that permit visual inspection of the covered area.
Uses: Selected superficial wounds and protection of appropriate sites.
Limitation: They have limited absorbency and may be unsuitable for heavily exuding or infected wounds without an appropriate management plan.
The objective is to protect the wound, manage exudate, minimise contamination, support healing and avoid unnecessary tissue injury.
The key principles are:
Assess the wound and the patient's overall condition.
Use hand hygiene and appropriate aseptic technique.
Remove the old dressing gently.
Inspect the wound for healing, infection, bleeding and tissue changes.
Clean the wound using an appropriate solution when indicated.
Apply a suitable dressing based on the wound's characteristics.
Secure the dressing without compromising circulation or causing skin damage.
Document findings and arrange follow-up.
Important: The goal is not to make every wound completely dry. Wound healing generally benefits from an appropriate moisture balance.
A wound dressing set is used for:
Routine postoperative wound care.
Dressing traumatic wounds.
Cleaning and dressing selected infected wounds.
Managing wounds with exudate.
Protecting surgical incisions.
Dressing ulcers and selected chronic wounds.
Applying prescribed topical wound treatments.
Inspecting and documenting wound healing.
Changing dressings following procedures such as incision and drainage, when indicated.
The dressing technique and materials depend on wound type, contamination, depth, exudate, tissue condition and the treatment plan.

Inadequate wound support, trauma, infection or inappropriate dressing management may contribute to wound deterioration.
A wound dressing set itself has few absolute contraindications. The main precautions relate to the wound and the selected materials.
Avoid unnecessary manipulation of a fresh surgical incision.
Do not use a dressing material that is unsuitable for the wound or the patient's allergies.
Use an appropriate sterile technique for wounds requiring aseptic dressing.
Assess bleeding, wound separation and suspected deep infection before proceeding routinely.
Avoid aggressive cleaning that damages viable tissue.
Follow specialist guidance for complex wounds, burns, diabetic foot ulcers and wounds involving exposed structures.
A dressing does not replace definitive management of a deep abscess, uncontrolled bleeding, wound dehiscence or systemic infection.

When cleaning is indicated, use the prescribed solution and technique. For a simple clean surgical wound, sterile saline or another protocol-approved solution may be appropriate.
Avoid unnecessarily scrubbing healthy granulation tissue.
Select a dressing appropriate to the wound and exudate.
Handle the wound-contact surface without contaminating it.
Apply the dressing without unnecessary tension.
Secure it using suitable fixation material.
Ensure the dressing does not impair circulation or movement.
Dispose of waste safely.

Clean wounds from the cleaner area towards the more contaminated area, using a fresh swab for each pass where this technique is indicated.
Do not move a contaminated swab back over an area already cleaned.
Avoid touching sterile wound-contact surfaces.
Do not use the same swab repeatedly across the wound.
Use a different approach for contaminated wounds, deep cavities and wounds requiring packing, according to local protocols.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Do not assume that a stronger antiseptic is always better. Some antiseptics can damage viable tissue if used inappropriately.
The examiner may ask you to describe the wound before applying the dressing.
Record the following when relevant:
Anatomical site and laterality.
Wound type and likely cause.
Length, width and depth when appropriate.
Wound edge approximation or separation.
Tissue appearance, including granulation, slough or necrosis.
Exudate amount, colour, consistency and odour.
Surrounding skin condition.
Pain and tenderness.
Signs of infection or systemic illness.
Dressing material used and the patient's response.
For a deep, tunnelling or undermined wound, assessment should follow the relevant wound-care protocol and the clinician's training.

blocks.text: The correct technique depends on the wound, patient risk, procedure and institutional guidelines. A dressing set should be used in accordance with the intended level of asepsis.
Q1. Identify this instrument or set.
This is a wound dressing set, used for wound inspection, cleaning, application of dressings and protection of the wound.
Q2. Name five components.
Dressing forceps, sterile gauze swabs, dressing pads, a gallipot and a kidney dish. A particular pack may contain additional or different items.
Q3. What is the function of dressing forceps?
To handle gauze, dressings and other materials while reducing direct contact with the wound and sterile items.
Q4. What is the purpose of a gallipot?
It holds a small quantity of a prescribed solution or other material during the dressing procedure.
Q5. What should you do if the old dressing is adherent?
Moisten it with an appropriate solution and remove it gently to avoid damaging the wound bed.
Q6. What are the main principles of wound dressing?
Appropriate hand hygiene, aseptic technique, careful wound assessment, suitable cleaning when indicated, appropriate dressing selection and accurate documentation.
Q7. Name four complications of poor wound dressing technique.
Infection, maceration, skin damage, tissue trauma and delayed wound healing.
Q8. Should every wound be cleaned with an antiseptic?
No. The cleaning solution should be selected according to the wound, the product's suitability and the clinical protocol. Sterile saline is appropriate for many routine wound-cleaning situations.
Q9. What features suggest wound infection?
Increasing pain, erythema, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge, wound deterioration or systemic features such as fever.
Q10. What should be documented after dressing a wound?
The wound's appearance, dimensions when relevant, exudate, surrounding skin, dressing applied, patient's response and any concerns or follow-up plan.
Before completing the station, ensure you can:
Identify the dressing set and label its components.
Distinguish plain dressing forceps from toothed dissecting forceps.
Explain the purpose of the gallipot, kidney dish, gauze and dressing pads.
Describe sterile-field preparation and aseptic non-touch technique.
Demonstrate safe removal of an old dressing.
Inspect and document wound characteristics.
Select an appropriate dressing and cleaning solution.
Recognise infection, maceration, bleeding and wound dehiscence.
Explain safe waste disposal and post-procedure documentation.
Dressing forceps: Used to handle swabs and dressings.
Gallipot: Holds a small quantity of solution.
Kidney dish: Receives used materials.
Aseptic non-touch technique: Protects key parts and key sites from contamination.
Wound care: Select the dressing according to the wound; avoid unnecessary trauma and inappropriate antiseptic use.
